- pr-review-toolkit:code-reviewer: Use this agent when you need to review code for adherence to project guidelines, style guides, and best practices. This agent should be used proactively after writing or modifying code, especially before committing changes or creating pull requests. It will check for style violations, potential issues, and ensure code follows the established patterns in CLAUDE.md. Also the agent needs to know which files to focus on for the review. In most cases this will be recently completed work which is unstaged in git (can be retrieved by running git diff). However there can be cases where this is different, make sure to specify this as the agent input when calling the agent. Typical triggers include the user asking for a review of a feature they just implemented, the assistant proactively reviewing its own newly-written code before declaring a task done, and a final pre-PR check before opening a pull request. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)

- pr-review-toolkit:comment-analyzer: Use this agent when you need to analyze code comments for accuracy, completeness, and long-term maintainability. This includes (1) after generating large documentation comments or docstrings, (2) before finalizing a pull request that adds or modifies comments, (3) when reviewing existing comments for potential technical debt or comment rot, and (4) when you need to verify that comments accurately reflect the code they describe. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)

This agent should be invoked proactively after completing a logical chunk of work that involves error handling, catch blocks, fallback logic, or any code that could potentially suppress errors. Examples:

Specifically use it (1) when introducing a new type to ensure it follows best practices for encapsulation and invariant expression, (2) during pull request creation to review all types being added, and (3) when refactoring existing types to improve their design quality. The agent will provide both qualitative feedback and quantitative ratings on encapsulation, invariant expression, usefulness, and enforcement. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

- zm-orchestrator: Scope and spec-conformance checker for an in-flight Zimmermann build. Use after an implementation step to judge whether the work delivers exactly what the plan specified — neither less nor more. Reports a verdict; never edits code. (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash)

- zm-planner: Synthesises gathered evidence into an executable build plan for a Zimmermann PWA Kit story. Use after all sources have been gathered, when the findings need to become a sequenced plan with per-step pass criteria. Does not gather evidence itself and does not write code. (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash, WebFetch)

- zm-scorer: Scores an implemented and tested Zimmermann build step and decides PASS or return-to-implementer. Use after the Tester reports. Judges quality against six axes; never edits code. (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash)

**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

- Bridge code and design via Code Connect (get_code_connect_map, add_code_connect_map)
- Create diagrams and FigJam content (generate_diagram, get_figjam)

- playwright-skill: Complete browser automation with Playwright. Auto-detects dev servers, writes clean test scripts to /tmp. Test pages, fill forms, take screenshots, check responsive design, validate UX, test login flows, check links, automate any browser task. Use when user wants to test websites, automate browser interactions, validate web functionality, or perform any browser-based testing.
- zimmerMANNBuild: The builder. Executes an approved zimmerMANNPreBuild plan through a closed-loop multi-agent workflow — implement, test, scope-check, score, rework until passed — committing each step and handing off to zimmerMANNPostBuild. Also handles rework from CodeRabbit or reviewer change requests after a PR is open.
- zimmerMANNDevImprover: Looks back over completed build work and improves the build chain. Reads the session transcripts and run artefacts for named stories, diagnoses where the loop failed and whose gap it was, checks whether the skills still cite things that are true, and proposes concrete edits to the build skills and loop agents — applied only on Marcel's explicit go.
- zimmerMANNDevOps: Runs deploys, promotions across environments, tags, release cuts and rollbacks on the Zimmermann PWA Kit. Verifies pipeline state live before every action, shows what each environment is running, and executes only on explicit approval. Reports broken gates and stops rather than working around them.
- zimmerMANNPostBuild: The senior dev pass after a build. Audits what zimmerMANNBuild produced against zimmerMANNPreBuild's plan and findings, runs a whole-feature sweep for uniform defects, writes the PR body, and owns the review conversation — pushing and replying only on Marcel's go.
- zimmerMANNPreBuild: The gate and planner before any Zimmermann PWA Kit build work. Gathers and cross-checks every source — Jira, Confluence, the FED handbook, the codebase and Figma — flags every gap and misalignment, then produces an executable closed-loop build plan and hands off to zimmerMANNBuild. Use at the start of any story, ticket or build task.
- zimmerMANNReview: Reviews someone else's PR as FED Lead. Establishes ground truth, fans out audit angles, verifies every finding before it is raised, then presents for adjudication — Marcel decides the verdict, and comments post only on his go. Loops until the PR is approved.
- zimmerMANNRevImprover: Looks back over completed PR reviews and improves how Marcel reviews. Reads the PR outcome and the review session transcript to judge whether each finding held up, whether anything was missed, and how the review was actually conducted — then proposes concrete edits to zimmerMANNReview, applied only on his explicit go.
- zimmerMANNSprinter: The skill for sprint and agile ceremonies as FED Lead — backlog refinement, sprint planning, standups, retros, and prep for any meeting. Reads Jira and Confluence, drafts what you need to take into the room, and writes to Jira only on your explicit go.
- audit-tier: Identify the protection tier, owner, and import blast radius of a file or directory under overrides/. Use before editing anything you're unsure about.
- code-quality: Audit recently changed or specified files for code quality issues — naming, circular imports, TypeScript coverage, test/story existence, and structural debt. Read-only. Use after implementing a feature or before opening a PR.
- code-review: AI-powered code review using CodeRabbit. Default code-review skill. Trigger for any explicit review request AND autonomously when the agent thinks a review is needed (code/PR/quality/security).
- contentful-register-component: Register a Zimmermann React component with Contentful Studio Experiences. Use when a developer asks to register, add, or expose a React component to Contentful, or when they need to create a Contentful component definition for an existing component.
- feature-spec: Turn a plain-English feature request into a scoped implementation plan before any code is written. Asks one clarifying question at a time, then produces a spec Claude Code can execute safely. Use this before starting any non-trivial implementation session.
- generate-changelog: Generate a release changelog from conventional commits and upstream baseline notes. Produces audience-specific outputs for the dev team, QA, product, and GitHub Release. Use before cutting a release branch or when preparing release notes.
- new-component: Scaffold a new Zimmermann component under overrides/app/components/ — TypeScript, Chakra-first, with a paired Storybook story. Use whenever a new custom component is needed.
- onboarding: Interactive onboarding for new developers and QA engineers joining the Zimmermann PWA Kit project. Asks role at the start, checks the mechanical setup items, then orients the person to the rules and tools relevant to their role and squad. Run this in the first Claude Code session on a new machine or a first day on the project.
- pr-checklist: Generate a PR description and merge checklist based on the files changed on the current branch. Pairs with /code-quality.
- project-init: One-time project setup walkthrough. Runs the state detection script, fixes automatable items, asks one question at a time for human-input items, and updates the 7.1c CI/CD & Environment Setup Checklist Confluence page as each item is confirmed. Run this once when setting up the project for the first time, or when returning to check setup status.
- qa-generate: Generate a Gherkin .feature file and Playwright test spec from a Jira story. Human-in-the-lead — Lead QA validates the .feature before Playwright is generated. Use for any new storefront user journey that needs E2E test coverage.
- scope-check: Review a proposed Claude Code prompt for scope safety before it runs. Classifies every likely-touched file by tier and verdicts the prompt SAFE / RISKY / BLOCKED, rewriting it when needed.
- session-start: Run the mandatory session start ritual — reads tracking docs, runs branch + health checks, states current position. Use at the start of every coding session.
- upstream-sync-review: Review the release notes / changelog for a new @salesforce/retail-react-app version before bumping. Lightweight policy — see .docs/upstreamPolicy.md.
- agent-sdk-dev:new-sdk-app: Create and setup a new Claude Agent SDK application
- claude-md-management:revise-claude-md: Update CLAUDE.md with learnings from this session
- code-review:code-review: Code review a pull request
- commit-commands:clean_gone: Cleans up all git branches marked as [gone] (branches that have been deleted on the remote but still exist locally), including removing associated worktrees.
- commit-commands:commit-push-pr: Commit, push, and open a PR
- commit-commands:commit: Create a git commit
- feature-dev:feature-dev: Guided feature development with codebase understanding and architecture focus
- plugin-dev:create-plugin: Guided end-to-end plugin creation workflow with component design, implementation, and validation
- pr-review-toolkit:review-pr: Comprehensive PR review using specialized agents
- ralph-loop:cancel-ralph: Cancel active Ralph Loop
- ralph-loop:help: Explain Ralph Loop plugin and available commands

- vercel:bootstrap: Bootstrap a repository with Vercel-linked resources by running preflight checks, provisioning integrations, verifying env keys, and then executing db/dev startup commands safely.
- vercel:deploy: Deploy the current project to Vercel. Pass "prod" or "production" as argument to deploy to production. Default is preview deployment.
- vercel:env: Manage Vercel environment variables. Commands include list, pull, add, remove, and diff. Use to sync environment variables between Vercel and your local development environment.
- vercel:status: Show the status of the current Vercel project — recent deployments, linked project info, and environment overview.
- claude-code-setup:claude-automation-recommender: Analyze a codebase and recommend Claude Code automations (hooks, subagents, skills, plugins, MCP servers). Use when user asks for automation recommendations, wants to optimize their Claude Code setup, mentions improving Claude Code workflows, asks how to first set up Claude Code for a project, or wants to know what Claude Code features they should use.
- claude-md-management:claude-md-improver: Audit and improve CLAUDE.md files in repositories. Use when user asks to check, audit, update, improve, or fix CLAUDE.md files. Scans for all CLAUDE.md files, evaluates quality against templates, outputs quality report, then makes targeted updates. Also use when the user mentions "CLAUDE.md maintenance" or "project memory optimization".
- figma:figma-code-connect: Creates and maintains Figma Code Connect template files that map Figma components to code snippets. Use when the user mentions Code Connect, Figma component mapping, design-to-code translation, or asks to create/update .figma.ts or .figma.js files.
- figma:figma-create-new-file: **MANDATORY prerequisite** — you MUST invoke this skill BEFORE every `create_new_file` tool call. NEVER call `create_new_file` directly without loading this skill first. Trigger whenever the user wants a new blank Figma file — a new design, FigJam, or Slides file — or when you need a fresh file before calling `use_figma`. Usage — /figma-create-new-file [editorType] [fileName] (e.g. /figma-create-new-file figjam My Whiteboard, /figma-create-new-file slides Q3 Review)
- figma:figma-design-to-code: **MANDATORY prerequisite** — you MUST invoke this skill BEFORE calling the `get_design_context` Figma MCP tool. You MUST trigger this skill whenever the user wants to implement, build, port, or code up a Figma design as code. Example prompts (not exhaustive) are 'implement this Figma design', 'build this screen from Figma', 'turn this Figma into code', 'design to code'. This skill provides critical instructions and steps to the agent on how to correctly implement Figma designs in code and must NOT be skipped.
- figma:figma-generate-design: Use this skill alongside figma-use when the task involves translating an application page, view, or multi-section layout into Figma. Triggers: 'write to Figma', 'create in Figma from code', 'push page to Figma', 'take this app/page and build it in Figma', 'create a screen', 'build a landing page in Figma', 'update the Figma screen to match code', 'convert this modal/dialog/drawer/panel to Figma'. This is the preferred workflow skill whenever the user wants to build or update a full page, modal, dialog, drawer, sidebar, panel, or any composed multi-section view in Figma from code or a description. Discovers design system components, variables, and styles from Code Connect files, existing screens, and library search, then imports them and assembles views incrementally section-by-section using design system tokens instead of hardcoded values.
- figma:figma-generate-diagram: MANDATORY prerequisite — load this skill BEFORE every `generate_diagram` tool call. NEVER call `generate_diagram` directly without loading this skill first. Trigger whenever the user asks to create, generate, draw, render, sketch, or build a diagram — flowchart, architecture diagram, sequence diagram, ERD or entity-relationship diagram, state diagram or state machine, gantt chart, or timeline. Also trigger when the user mentions Mermaid syntax or wants a system architecture, decision tree, dependency graph, API call flow, auth handshake, schema, or pipeline visualized in FigJam. Routes to type-specific guidance, sets universal Mermaid constraints, and tells you when to use a different diagram type or skip the tool entirely (mindmaps, pie charts, class diagrams, etc.).
- figma:figma-generate-library: Build or update a professional-grade design system in Figma from a codebase. Use when the user wants to create variables/tokens, build component libraries, create individual components with proper variant sets and variable bindings, set up theming (light/dark modes), document foundations, or reconcile gaps between code and Figma. Also use when the user asks to create or generate any component in Figma — even a single one — since components require proper variable foundations, variant states, and design token bindings to be production-quality. This skill teaches WHAT to build and in WHAT ORDER — it complements the `figma-use` skill which teaches HOW to call the Plugin API. Both skills should be loaded together.

## Modes

| Mode | Does |
|---|---|
| `status` *(default)* | Full state. A bare invocation stops here. |
| `deploy <env> <ref>` | Preflight, then dispatch on approval |
| `promote <from> <to>` | Takes what `<from>` is running and deploys it to `<to>` |
| `tag <version>` | Validates the name, checks the tag workflow is even present, cuts on approval |
| `release` | The full cut — changelog, tag, promote |

**Two workflows are not dispatchable.** `deploy-dev.yml` fires only on push to `develop`.

```bash
for e in dev test sit uat staging prod; do
  gh api "repos/ZimmermannAU/zimmermann-pwa/deployments?environment=$e&per_page=1" \
    --jq 'if length==0 then "never deployed" else "\(.[0].ref) @ \(.[0].sha[:7]) — \(.[0].created_at[:10])" end'
done
```

Print all six with their age. **Flag staleness** — an environment weeks behind the one below it is
the context you would otherwise reconstruct by hand, and it changes whether a promotion is routine
or a leap.

### 2. Pipeline health

- **Environment protection rules** — `gh api repos/.../environments/<env>`. Report `protection_rules`
  and `deployment_branch_policy` honestly. As of the last check every environment returned `[]` and

|---|---|
| `dev` | not dispatchable — auto on push to `develop` |

| `master` | the Contentful environment |

`README.md:78` tells a tier-1 approver to set production env vars in the MRT console under `prod`.
**The target is `production`.** Production is the one tier with no automated var sync, so this is
the only path — use the right name.

---

## Executing

Nothing runs without approval. Present, then wait.

For **irreversible** actions, print the literal command and state the consequence plainly before
asking:

- **Any tag** — *"This tag cannot be deleted or moved by anyone, including you. The `tag-rc` ruleset
  has zero bypass actors."*
- **A deploy to `prod`** — *"No environment reviewer exists. `versionGuard` will "* + (skip this ref
  / block a downgrade), whichever is true for the ref in hand.
- **Any first-ever run of a workflow** — *"`deploy-stg.yml` has never executed. This is its first run."*

Then dispatch:

```bash
gh workflow run deploy-<env>.yml -f ref=<ref>
```

Report the run URL, watch it to completion, and report the real outcome — not the dispatch's exit code.

## Tagging

Before cutting any tag:

1. **Validate the name** against both patterns — `^v\d+\.\d+\.\d+-rc\.\d+$` and
   `^v\d+\.\d+\.\d+(-hotfix\.\d+)?$`. Nothing else is accepted anywhere, and **no layer matches
   anything but lowercase `v*`** — `V0.1.0` or `0.1.0` slips past the hook, the workflow and both
   rulesets.
2. **Check `tag-validate.yml` exists on the branch being tagged.** GitHub evaluates a tag workflow
   from the tagged commit; the file has historically lived only on `develop`, so a tag cut from a
   release branch is not validated at all. Say which is true right now.
3. **Annotated only** — `git tag -a <tag> -m "<message>"`. Never lightweight. Never `npm version`;
   its commit is blocked by `release/**` protection.
4. **Push the tag alone** — `git push origin <tag>`.

## Rollback

Both paths, and state the gap before either:

> `rollback=true` skips the version downgrade guard, and no environment required reviewer exists to
> catch a mistake. Nothing else is watching this.

- **Controlled** — `gh workflow run deploy-<env>.yml -f ref=<previous-tag> -f rollback=true`
- **Emergency** — re-activate the previous MRT bundle by hand, then
  `node scripts/versionGuard.mjs record <env> <ref>` so the Deployment record matches reality

## Release cut

1. `/generate-changelog` — the team's skill, and `tagging.md` says run it before cutting
2. Cut `release/vX.Y.Z` from `develop`
3. RC tags as needed, each deployed to `test`
4. Merge to `main`, bump `package.json` (Tier 1 — needs an approver)
5. Final `vX.Y.Z` tag on the merge commit — tier-1-approvers only
6. Promote `uat → staging → prod`
7. Back-merge to `develop` — required by `.docs/releaseBranchesRules.md`, enforced by nothing

Offer `/upstream-sync-review` when the upstream watcher has flagged a new base version.

---

## When a gate is broken

**Report it, name the owner, and stop.**

Do not work around it, do not fix it, do not draft the escalation. `.github/workflows/` and
environment configuration are **Tier 1**, owned by Integration / SI Partner, routed to
`@ZimmermannAU/tier-1-approvers` by `CODEOWNERS`. Not yours to change.

Give the evidence — the command, its real output, the file and line — so the report stands on its
own when Marcel takes it to whoever owns it.

---

## Hard rules

- **Never dispatch, tag, push or roll back without explicit approval.**
- **Never modify `.github/workflows/`, `config/`, `package.json`, `.claude/**` or any Tier 1 file.**
- **Never present cached state as current.** If you did not check it this run, say so.
- **Never claim a deploy succeeded from the dispatch's exit code.** Watch the run.
- **Never guess an MRT target name.** `production`, not `prod`.
- **Say what you could not verify** — MRT console state is not reachable from here, and that
  includes what production's env vars actually are.

      - name: Upload Playwright report

        with:

          path: playwright-report/
          retention-days: 30

      - name: Upload Pages artifact

        with:
          path: playwright-report/

  deploy-playwright-report:

    if: always()

/**
 * versionGuard.mjs — downgrade protection for tag-based environment promotion.
 *
 * On the GitHub Team plan, a deploy's auto-created Deployment records the *trigger*
 * ref (the default branch), NOT the tag that was actually deployed. So we record the
 * deployed tag ourselves (an explicit GitHub Deployment) and read it back here to
 * block accidental downgrades on the manually-promoted tiers (test/uat/staging/prod).
 *
 * Usage (from a deploy-*.yml, after `npm install`, with GH_TOKEN set):
 *   node scripts/versionGuard.mjs check  <env> <ref>   # before push — block a downgrade
 *   node scripts/versionGuard.mjs record <env> <ref>   # after a successful push — record the tag
 *
 * <env> is the GitHub Environment name (test | uat | staging | prod).
 *
 * `check` behaviour:
 *   - <ref> is not a version tag       -> skip/allow (e.g. deploying a feature branch to Test)
 *   - <ref> not valid semver           -> fail closed (exit 1)
 *   - no prior tag on the env          -> allow (first deploy)
 *   - <ref> strictly older             -> BLOCK (exit 1)
 *   - <ref> equal or newer             -> allow
 *   - lookup error / invalid stored ref -> fail closed (exit 1)
 *
 * `record` skips non-version-tag refs; it FAILS the run if it cannot create the deployment record
 * (a missing baseline would let a later run downgrade), and only warns if the follow-up status
 * update fails (the ref is already recorded, which is what the guard reads).
 */
import {execFileSync} from 'node:child_process'
import semver from 'semver'

// vX.Y.Z with an optional -rc.N or -hotfix.N suffix (matches the repo tag rulesets).

const repo = process.env.GITHUB_REPOSITORY

const die = (msg) => {

}

    console.log(`✓ version-guard: ${msg}`)
    process.exit(0)
}

}

/** Run `gh` and return stdout. Optional `input` is written to stdin. Throws on non-zero exit. */
function gh(args, input) {
    return execFileSync('gh', args, {encoding: 'utf8', input})
}

 * Pages through deployments (newest-first) so a long run of non-version (branch) deploys can't bury
 * the last tag record. Skips non-version refs; fails closed if a version-shaped ref is not valid
 * semver (so a malformed baseline like `v01.2.3` can't crash the compare or slip a downgrade through).

## Pipeline status — derived live, 2026-08-31

### The ladder

**The `deployments` API is not trustworthy here.** Five workflows declare an `environment:` without deploying any code, and GitHub logs a Deployment record for each. The table below is built from **`deploy-*.yml` run history only**:

| Env | Actually running | Deployed | Drift vs `develop` |
|---|---|---|---|
| `dev` | `269d5d4` | 28 Aug | current |
| `test` | `04039a9` | 28 Aug | **13 commits behind** |
| `sit` | **never deployed** | — | `deploy-sit.yml`: 1 run, *skipped* |
| `uat` | `d9c3c40` | 11 Aug | **170 commits behind, 20 days** |
| `staging` | **never deployed** | — | `deploy-stg.yml` never run |
| `prod` | **never deployed** | — | `deploy-prod.yml` never run |

What the raw API would have told you instead: `sit` running `develop@d9c3c40` from 10 Aug — that record is an **env-var sync** by `vtcrisostomo`, not a deploy. And `test`'s newest record (30 Aug, `TimLavelleACC`) is a **BrowserStack preview run**. Both are phantoms.

The contaminating workflows:

```
qa.yml                       → environment: dev
teardown-preview.yml         → environment: dev
e2e-browserstack-preview.yml → environment: test
sync-env-vars-to-mrt.yml     → environment: ${{ inputs.target }}   (sit/uat/staging)
```

`deploy-preview.yml` carries a comment showing this exact problem was already found and fixed **for that one workflow**. The other four were never cleaned up.

**The version guard is not affected.** `scripts/versionGuard.mjs:57` pages newest-first and skips any ref that isn't `v*`, with 2000 deployments of headroom. Every phantom record is `ref=develop`, so all are skipped. The guard is sound — it's the human-readable ladder that lies.

### Gates

**SIT Gate cannot pass.** Its one and only run (5 Aug, `release/v0.1.0`) failed:

| Job | Result |
|---|---|
| Playwright P0 journeys | **failure** |
| Lighthouse CI | **failure** |
| Publish Playwright report to Pages | failure (consequence) |
| Bundle size check | success |
| MuleSoft contract tests | success |

Two independent causes, both still true right now:

- **P0** — the `p0` project exists (`playwright.config.js:53`, `testMatch: ['**/*.p0.spec.{js,ts}']`) but **zero `*.p0.spec` files exist**. Separately, `digital-sit.yml:22` reads `RETAIL_APP_HOME: ${{ vars.RETAIL_APP_HOME }}` from a job with **no `environment:` key**, so it reads repo-level variables — of which there are **zero**. `RETAIL_APP_HOME` exists only on the `test` environment, which that job cannot see.
- **Lighthouse** — `LHCI_SERVER_BASE_URL`, `LHCI_TOKEN`, `LHCI_TARGET_URL_SIT` are all **absent**.

Consequence: `release/**` merges are blocked, and `deploy-sit.yml` can never fire — it triggers on a *successful* `SIT Gate` `workflow_run`.

**No environment has any protection.** All six return `protection_rules=[]` and `deployment_branch_policy=null`. Nothing stands between a dispatch and production.

### Release / tag state — this corrects my earlier notes

I told you at session start there were no tags and no release branch. That was stale; both now exist:

- **`release/v0.1.0` exists** — and is dead weight: **0 commits ahead** of `develop`, **188 behind**, last commit 3 Aug.
- **Tag `v0.1.0-rc.0` exists** — annotated, yours, on `226c71d` (the release-branch tip).
- **`tag-validate.yml` is ABSENT at that tag and on `release/v0.1.0`** — it lives only on `develop`. GitHub evaluates a tag workflow from the tagged commit, so **that tag was never validated by anything**. This is exactly the failure mode the skill warns about, and it explains why `tag-validate.yml` shows *never run* despite a tag existing.

Also confirmed: **every deployment to date used `ref=develop`**. The first tag-based promotion will be the first time the "no branch refs above `test`" rule has ever bitten.

### Other verified facts

- **`prod` has zero environment variables.** MRT console is the only path, and the target name is `production`, not `prod`.
- `bundlesize` **is** declared in `package.json` — the skill's note that it isn't is wrong. `cross-env` and `lhci` are transitive; all three currently resolve in `node_modules/.bin`.

### Broken gates — owner, not mine to fix

The SIT Gate blockers live in `.github/workflows/` and environment configuration — **Tier 1, Integration / SI Partner**, routed to `@ZimmermannAU/tier-1-approvers` by CODEOWNERS. Evidence above is reproducible: `gh api .../actions/runs/30982818501/jobs`, `gh secret list`, `gh variable list`, `find e2e -name '*.p0.spec.*'`.

### What I could not verify

**MRT console state.** What bundle is actually *active* on each MRT target, and what production's environment variables really contain, is not reachable from here. The table above reflects what CI pushed, not what MRT is serving — a hand-activated bundle would not show up.
